To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a) the prevalence of androgen receptors in prostate cancer is similar to that found in benign prostate hyperplasia, b) there is no difference in the level of androgen receptors found in prostate cancer and benign prostate hyperplastic tissue, c) there is no association between androgen receptors and survival in prostate cancers treated by hormone therapy, d) there is a positive association between cytoploplasmic oestrogens receptors and time to progression of prostate cancers treated by hormonal therapy.
cytoplasmic estrogen receptors are associated with a better prognosis.

the prevalence of oestrogen receptor in prostate carcinoma is 50% (range 30%-70%) and the prevalence of cytosol oesrogen receptor in prostate cancer is 50% and is not associated with survival but is associated with progression-free interval.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the prevalence of androgen and oestradiol receptors in the prostate and the relationship between receptor status and time to progression and duration of survival in patients with prostatic adenocarcinoma treated by hormone manipulation.
the role of androgen and oestradiol receptors in prostate cancer.
the study of the androgen receptor in the prostate and the effect of its manipulation on the outcome of the disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
receptor analysis of TUR chips is not of any value in the diagnosis or prognosis of prostate cancer.
the presence or absence of any of the prostate cancer receptors has little or no influence on time to disease progression or survival in patients treated with hormonal manipulation.
receptor analysis in prostate disease is not of value in the management of the patient.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the presence of receptors is not a reliable indicator of malignancy in the prostate, but may be useful in the assessment of prognosis of patients who have already been diagnosed with prostate cancer.
the presence of ANR and OCR in prostate cancer is not a prognostic factor for survival or progression-free interval.
there is no evidence that receptor status is of prognostic importance in prostate cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a need to standardize and validate the use of TURP chips as an alternative to biopsy.
there is a lack of evidence for the use of receptor status in prostate cancer.
the cytosol oestradiol receptor may have a prognostic effect in prostate cancer, with regard to the time taken to progress on hormone manipulation, but not survival.
